text: Linda Lingle (née Cutter; June 4, 1953) is an American politician and publisher who served as the sixth governor of Hawaii from 2002 to 2010. A member of the Republican Party, she was the first Republican elected governor of Hawaii since 1959 and the state's first female and Jewish governor. Prior to her gubernatorial service, she served as mayor of Maui County from 1991 to 1999 and as chair of the Hawaii Republican Party from 1999 to 2002. As of 2025[update], Lingle and her lieutenant governor, Duke Aiona, are the last Republicans to have won or held statewide office in Hawaii. During the 2004 Republican National Convention in New York City, she served as chair during the absence of Dennis Hastert. In 2012, she was the Republican nominee for the United States Senate, losing to Mazie Hirono in a race for an open seat vacated by retiring U.S. Senator Daniel Akaka. She is the only woman to have served as Hawaii's governor. Born Linda Cutter to a Jewish family in St. Louis, Missouri in 1953, the daughter of Mildred and Richard Cutter, she moved to Southern California at age 12, graduated from Birmingham High School in Lake Balboa, California, and earned a bachelor's degree in journalism cum laude from California State University, Northridge in 1975. She moved to Hawaii shortly after, working initially in Honolulu as a public information officer for the Teamsters and Hotel Workers Union, then starting the Molokai Free Press on Molokai. In 1980, she was elected to the Maui County Council, serving five two-year terms—three representing Molokai and two as an at-large member—and won the mayoral election in 1991 at age 37, becoming the youngest and first woman to hold the office. She was re-elected in 1994. Under her leadership, Maui County implemented performance-based budgeting, earning her the Distinguished Budget Presentation Award from the Government Finance Officers Association for four years, and she is credited with attracting tourism and job growth during a period of state-wide economic struggle. In 1998, she ran against incumbent Governor Benjamin J. Cayetano, losing by a single percentage point in the closest election in Hawaii history, after which she became chair of the Hawaii Republican Party, overhauling party policies and increasing Republican representation in the state legislature, with the party holding 19 of 51 seats in the state House at its peak. After Cayetano retired in 2002, Lingle was selected as the Republican nominee for governor, aided by the withdrawal of Democratic mayor Jeremy Harris over campaign finance allegations. She ran on a platform called "Agenda for New Beginnings," promoting Republican leadership and criticizing past Democratic governance. She won the election with former state judge Duke Aiona as her lieutenant governor. She was inaugurated in the rotunda of the Hawaii State Capitol, taking the oath on a Tanakh, and was the first state governor-elect not to be inaugurated at the Coronation Pavilion of Iolani Palace. She signed into law the Three Strikes Law and Sex Offender Registry Website Law and vetoed a bill requiring hospitals to provide emergency contraception to rape victims, citing concerns about Catholic hospitals challenging it. In May 2004, she led a delegation to Israel, paid for by the Israeli government. She enjoyed high approval ratings, typically around 70 percent. In 2004, she campaigned for Republican candidates in the presidential and state legislative races, supporting President George W. Bush's Iraq policies and helping to boost Republican efforts in Hawaii, though Kerry won the state and Republicans lost five legislative seats. In January 2006, she received an honorary doctorate in public management from the University of the City of Manila. She attempted to divide the State Board of Education into seven local boards but failed. One of her more controversial initiatives was opposing the construction of a new prison in Hawaii, advocating instead for sending prisoners to the mainland. In 2006, she announced her re-election bid, defeating former state senator Randy Iwase in the primary and winning the general election with 63 percent of the vote, the largest margin in state history. In August 2007, the Hawaii Supreme Court invalidated a law exempting the Hawaii Superferry from environmental assessment, though the ferry operated to Kauai without one and was met by protesters; Lingle responded with a massive police and Coast Guard response and claimed protesters could be charged under anti-terrorism laws. She sought a legislative exemption (Act Two) for the Superferry, which was challenged as unconstitutional and later struck down by the Hawaii Supreme Court in March 2009. In 2008, she delivered a primetime address at the Republican National Convention praising Sarah Palin's nomination as vice-presidential candidate, highlighting their shared status as Republican women governors of non-contiguous states and their connection through the Republican Governors Association. In July 2009, her administration ended the Hawaiʻi Immigrant Health Initiative, eliminating medical coverage for legal immigrants with fewer than five years of presence and Compact of Free Association residents from QUEST, prompting a federal preliminary injunction from Judge John Michael Seabright, with subsequent plans by Governor Neil Abercrombie to appeal to the Ninth Circuit. On April 13 and 14, 2010, two student protesters and eight others were arrested for occupying her office and protesting a school furlough policy due to budget shortfalls. On July 6, 2010, she vetoed Hawaii House Bill 444, which would have allowed civil unions, arguing the issue should be decided by referendum; the bill passed the state senate but fell short of the two-thirds threshold in the state house. Ineligible to run for a third term, she left office on December 6, 2010, succeeding Democrat Neil Abercrombie and becoming the second Republican governor in state history after William F. Quinn (1959–1962), and the only GOP candidate to be re-elected governor of Hawaii by popular vote. In October 2011, she announced her intent to run for the U.S. Senate seat vacated by Daniel Akaka, winning the Republican primary on August 11, 2012, and facing Hirono in the general election. She was the first well-funded Republican to run for the Senate in Hawaii since Pat Saiki in 1990 and the strongest Republican candidate for a full term in memory, though Hirono won with 63 percent of the vote to her 37 percent. After her Senate bid, she taught a public policy seminar at California State University, Northridge and worked with the Governor's Council and Energy Security Council for the Bipartisan Policy Center. In January 2015, she was appointed senior adviser to Illinois Governor Bruce Rauner, joining a trio of outsiders to address retirement systems and credit ratings, and left the position in July 2016. In 2016, she delivered an opening-day speech at the Republican National Convention on Jewish support for the party and Donald Trump. In January 2017, she announced her plan to move back to Hawaii in April 2017, joining Harvard University's group of former governors to discuss the opioid crisis in May 2017, and becoming a member of Hawaii Pacific University's board of trustees in June 2017, serving through 2020. In December 2018, she was the last speaker in a Leadership Series for the Nisei Veterans Memorial Center, describing leadership as developed through handling failure and seizing opportunities. She supported Rick Blangiardi, who won the 2020 mayoral election in Honolulu in January 2021. In 2022, she led the "Women's Prison Project" to reform women's processing in Hawaii's criminal justice system, helping open housing for women leaving prison in 2023, and established a Hawaii Pacific University scholarship in her name for students with potential for exceptional leadership. She was married and divorced twice: first to Charles Lingle in 1972, divorced in 1975, and later to Maui attorney William Crockett from 1986 to 1997; she is currently single with no children. Her uncle founded the Cutter Ford car dealerships in Hawaiʻi. She is a California State University, Northridge 2004 distinguished alumni honoree and served on the Honorary Delegation to accompany President George W. Bush to Jerusalem in May 2008 for the 60th anniversary of the State of Israel.
